name: Hanshin Koshien Stadium
why: Hanshin finished first in the Central League and host the Climax final here Oct 14–19. If they win it, the Series opens in the most sacred ballpark in Asia: ivy walls, black-dirt infield, 47,000 people singing the Rokko Oroshi. Bring a yellow towel, or buy one at the gate.
tips: Face-value tickets drop through team sites and Ticket Pia; resale runs higher
Your ceiling: $200 ≈ ¥31,700 per game
Tigers fan club presales usually go first — membership is being researched

name: Mizuho PayPay Dome Fukuoka
why: SoftBank clinched the Pacific League on Sept 17 and start the Climax final with a built-in edge. If they hold, Games 3–5 are here, which puts you a short walk from Nakasu's yatai stalls after every game. Hard to script a better three days.
tips: Off day Oct 26: shinkansen Shin-Osaka → Hakata is about 2.5 hours
Dome roof means no rainouts
Sit near the right-field Hawks cheering section for the full show

name: Tokyo Dome
why: If the Giants upset Hanshin, the Series comes here. Either way, the Baseball Hall of Fame sits in the same complex, so it earns a visit.
tips: Giants vs DeNA first stage Oct 10–12, here

name: Yokohama Stadium
why: DeNA won the whole thing from third place in 2024. If they repeat the trick, you'll be next to Chinatown for Games 1–2.
tips: Five-minute walk to Yokohama Chinatown

name: Koshien History Museum
why: A century of the national high-school tournament and the Tigers. The kids' tournament is the heart of Japanese baseball; this explains why grown men cry over it.
tips: Combine with a game day; it closes early

name: Japanese Baseball Hall of Fame
why: Sadaharu Oh, Babe Ruth's 1934 tour, Ichiro, Ohtani. Small, dense and thoughtfully done.
tips: Inside the Tokyo Dome complex, gate 21

name: Oh Sadaharu Baseball Museum
localName: 王貞治ベースボールミュージアム
why: 868 home runs, one man. Next to the dome, so it fits a Fukuoka game day.
tips: Part of BOSS E・ZO FUKUOKA beside the dome

name: Daruma Kushikatsu, Shinsekai
why: Deep-fried skewers in Osaka's old neon district. Bourdain ate here. One rule, posted everywhere: no double-dipping in the communal sauce.
tips: Cabbage is free; use it to scoop sauce
Go after a Koshien game: 30 minutes by train

name: Dotonbori
why: Takoyaki, okonomiyaki and the giant moving crab sign. Touristy, loud and still the right place to eat badly and happily in Osaka.
tips: Eat standing; most stalls are cash-friendly
Tigers fans jump into the canal when they win big (don't)

name: Nakasu yatai stalls
why: Open-air food stalls along the river, eight stools each. Hakata tonkotsu ramen, oden, yakitori, strangers who become drinking partners. This is the post-game plan.
tips: Many stalls are cash only
Open evenings; closed in heavy rain

name: Bar Albatross, Golden Gai
why: Golden Gai is six alleys of bars that seat five or six people each. Bourdain drank at Albatross. Chandeliers in a closet, and the best people-watching in Shinjuku.
tips: Small cover charge is normal in Golden Gai
Some bars are regulars-only; look for English signs

name: Sarashina Horii
why: Soba made here since 1789, white and delicate. A Bourdain pick, and a calm counterweight to Shinjuku.
tips: Order the sarashina (white) soba first

name: Tsukiji Outer Market
why: The wholesale market moved, but the outer market stayed: tamagoyaki on a stick, uni bowls, knife shops. Go hungry at 8am.
tips: Many shops close by early afternoon

name: Omicho Market
why: Kanazawa's 300-year-old market: snow crab season starts Nov 6, nodoguro, sweet shrimp. Bourdain filmed here. A strong pick for the open stretch after the Series.
tips: Snow crab season opens Nov 6

name: Ramen Alley, Sapporo
localName: 元祖さっぽろラーメン横丁
why: A narrow lane of miso-ramen counters. Bourdain came through on No Reservations. Far north, but cheap flights make it a real option.

name: Fushimi Inari Taisha
why: Ten thousand vermilion gates climbing a mountain. Go at dawn and walk past the crowds to the top; above the halfway point you'll be nearly alone with the foxes.
tips: Open 24 hours
Full loop to the summit: 2–3 hours

name: Todai-ji
why: A 15-metre bronze Buddha in one of the largest wooden buildings on earth, rebuilt and still standing since 1709. The deer will bow for crackers.
tips: Easy day trip from Osaka or Kyoto

name: Himeji Castle
why: The real thing: an original castle that survived war and bombing. Stop on the way from Kansai toward Fukuoka on the Oct 26 travel day.
tips: Price rose for non-residents in 2026; verify at the gate
On the shinkansen line between Osaka and Hakata

name: Itsukushima Shrine, Miyajima
why: The floating torii. Stay one night so you see it after the day-trippers leave. Pair with Hiroshima's Peace Memorial.
tips: Island visitor tax ¥100
Momijidani maple valley peaks mid-November

name: Dazaifu Tenmangu
why: A 1,100-year-old shrine 30 minutes from Fukuoka. Eat a hot umegae-mochi on the approach. Easy morning before a night game.
tips: Nishitetsu train from Tenjin

name: Kiyomizu-dera
why: A wooden stage over a hillside of maples, built without nails. Crowded, and worth it anyway.
tips: Autumn night illumination usually starts mid-November

name: Kumano Kodo (Nakahechi)
why: A thousand-year pilgrim trail through cedar forest to the Kumano shrines. Two to four days, inn to inn. One of only two pilgrim routes on the World Heritage list.
tips: Book minshuku lodging a few days ahead
Pairs naturally with a Koyasan temple stay

name: Kamikochi
why: An alpine valley under 3,000-metre peaks, with the larches turning gold. The road closes Nov 15, so early November is the last window of the year.
tips: Private cars banned; bus or taxi from Hirayu or Sawando
Season closes Nov 15

name: Mount Takao
why: An hour from Shinjuku, a 599-metre mountain with a temple near the top and Fuji views on a clear day. Good first-day leg-stretcher after the flight.
tips: Trail 6 is the quieter, wetter route up

name: Lake Biwa bass fishing
why: Japan's biggest lake and a famous big-bass fishery. Several guides run English-language solo trips. Close to Kyoto.
tips: Look for guides that list English and solo bookings
Prices are per boat; ask about half days

name: Genkai Sea shared charters
why: Shared boats out of Fukuoka-area ports target sea bream, yellowtail and squid. You can join solo as one seat on a shared boat. Fits the Fukuoka leg.
tips: Shared (乗合) boats take individuals
Most captains speak little English; a translation app helps

name: Koyasan temple stay
why: Sleep in a working Buddhist temple on a mountain, eat the monks' vegetarian shojin ryori, join the 6am chanting, then walk Okunoin cemetery at night among 200,000 graves and stone lanterns. This is your zen place.
tips: Price usually includes dinner and breakfast
About 2 hours from Osaka (Nankai line + cable car)

name: Hiiragiya Ryokan
why: A 200-year-old ryokan where Bourdain stayed. Tatami, a wooden bath, a kaiseki dinner served in the room. The once-in-a-trip splurge.
tips: Per person with dinner; book ahead
Splurge candidate: yes or no still open

name: Takinoya, Noboribetsu
why: Hokkaido's sulfur-steaming onsen town. Bourdain stayed at Takinoya on No Reservations. A splurge if you head north.

name: Jidai Matsuri
why: Two thousand people in costume, from every era of Kyoto's 1,000 years as capital, parade to Heian Shrine.
tips: Arrival day; realistic only if you land early and go straight to Kyoto

name: Kurama Fire Festival
why: Torches the size of logs carried through a mountain village at night. One of Japan's wildest festivals.
tips: Has been scaled back in recent years; confirm it's on
Same night as Jidai Matsuri

name: Karatsu Kunchi
why: Giant lacquered floats (a sea bream, a samurai helmet, a dragon) hauled through town by chanting crews. Starts the day after Game 7, an hour from Fukuoka. This could be the bridge from the Series to the open weeks.
tips: Nov 3 is the big day on the beach
Lodging in Karatsu fills; stay in Fukuoka and train in

name: Hakone Daimyo Procession
why: A feudal lord's procession of 170 people in Edo-period dress walks through the hot-spring town.

name: Tokyo Jidai Matsuri
why: Asakusa's costume parade through Tokyo history, around Senso-ji.

name: Japan Alps larches
why: High-country larch turns gold first. Early November catches the end.

name: Nikko · Irohazaka
why: Lake Chuzenji and the hairpin road peak in late October; the town and Toshogu shrine follow into early November.

name: Oirase Gorge
why: A 14-kilometre stream walk under maples and beech. Far north, so it peaks early.

name: Korankei
why: Four thousand maples along a river near Nagoya. Starts turning right as your trip ends.

name: Kyoto temples
why: Eikando, Tofuku-ji, Arashiyama. Kyoto peaks late; your last days might catch the first wave.

name: Momijidani, Miyajima
why: Maple Valley behind the shrine. The name says it.
